title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation scam in which fraudulent emails falsely present themselves as coming from a named public broadcaster and her production team. The messages are personalized to each recipient's actual work, which makes them more convincing than generic phishing attempts. Cybersecurity experts cited in the reporting attribute that personalization capacity, at least in part, to AI tools that lower the cost of crafting targeted fraudulent outreach at scale.

The failure is not inside a deployed AI product but in the use of AI as an instrument of fraud by outside actors. The point of vulnerability is the recipient's inbox, before any organizational system can intervene. A basic verification step, contacting the broadcaster through its official channels rather than replying to the incoming message, is the check that would have caught it, and one victim did apply that check after a payment request raised suspicion.

What is not established is who is running the scam, whether AI was definitively used or merely suspected by experts, and whether any investigation has produced findings or charges.

reports.title: ‘Too good to be true?’: No, WHYY’s Terry Gross did not personally email you to be a guest on ‘Fresh Air’
Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

summary:
# Summary

A wave of fraudulent emails has targeted authors, entertainers, and public figures by impersonating Terry Gross and the Fresh Air production team. The scammers send highly personalized messages referencing the recipient's work and proposing interviews, eventually requesting payment of several hundred dollars for supposed production costs. One university history professor received such an email and initially believed it was legitimate until a follow-up message asked for $250, prompting her to contact WHYY security and launch an investigation.

According to cybersecurity experts, artificial intelligence has enabled scammers to create convincing, personalized impersonations more cheaply than before. WHYY, NPR, and law enforcement are investigating the matter and have confirmed they never charge guests for interviews. Red flags include requests for payment and suspicious email addresses like terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com. Experts recommend verifying interview invitations through official organizational contacts rather than responding to suspicious messages.
